item.title: The Smartest Part of a Home Camera Is Moving Off the Cloud
item.description:
For most of the decade gone by, the “smart” aspect of smart camera systems resided on external hardware setups that belonged to someone else; i.e., a security firm owned the footage and any queries would be worked on behind the scenes, with the answer being sent back to the owner’s phone, usually for a monthly fee. 

However, this year, a series of events (particularly the unsettling Nancy Guthrie case) has shifted that status quo, leading many to question not only what a camera can and cannot recognize but also where that backend recognition work actually takes place.

AI features, priced per month

Regardless, the cloud-first model is still very much alive and kicking, with Google’s camera line now integrated into Google Home Premium, costing subscribers $10 or $20 a month. However, popular features such as Familiar Faces still require a further, special subscription (while Gemini-powered alerts and AI summaries also sit in a similar paid bracket).

And, even though such a setup might look unusual to some, it really isn’t. This is because recognizing faces, sorting clips and answering questions about footage takes computing power, and for years the easiest place to put that power was a data center billed back to the customer. 

The catch, that has now presented itself, however, is that every one of those features depends on footage leaving the house, being processed elsewhere and staying available only while the plan stays active.

The brains move into a box

With privacy concerns skyrocketing with each passing day, a growing consortium of security hardware manufacturers have been betting on the fact that buyers would much rather keep all of their cameras’ audio/video processing activities to the confines of their homes.

In this regard, this year’s iteration of CES saw Reolink preview a standalone hub built to handle local detection, search and processing, cutting out any cloud dependency entirely. Similarly, last month, smart home security giant EZVIZ used the IFA stage to pitch a local-first range that makes the cloud optional rather than mandatory, even though it continues to sell cloud storage and keeps some features online.

According the highly popular security camera and smart home brand Lorex, a highly popular its Connect V Series supports local recording without a mandatory cloud subscription, with detection features varying by model. Optional cloud backup is available, allowing owners to keep footage off-site as well as on their own equipment.

Local AI comes with homework

That being said, moving the entire aforementioned data stack in-house shifts a large chink of the responsibility onto the owner and a recorder that performs facial recognition is a far more valuable target than one that simply stores video. Consequently, firmware updates, strong unique passwords and keeping the device off the open internet matter more. 

Facial recognition also raises its own questions about recording neighbors and passersby, and the rules on that vary by state and country.

Still, the shape of the market has clearly changed because just a year or two ago, AI features were mostly a reason to sign up for a plan, but now, they are increasingly being built into the hardware itself, and buyers now have a real choice between renting a camera’s intelligence by the month or owning it outright. In any case, an interesting couple of years lie ahead for the industry!

(Photo by Jakub Zerdzicki)

item.title: Fake ChatGPT and Claude Apps Use Signed Executables to Install Yoba Malware
item.description:
Fake ChatGPT and Claude apps spread Yoba malware through GitHub, using signed executables to load a cryptominer on Windows PCs and support other payloads.

Attackers are distributing fake ChatGPT and Claude desktop applications through GitHub, packaging malware alongside genuine executables signed by OpenAI and Anthropic. The campaign came to light through research by Check Point, whose analysts observed cryptocurrency-mining software being installed on Windows computers through a loader capable of delivering other malware.

In its research, Check Point calls the campaign Yoba and describes fake GitHub projects offering supposed “GPT-5.6 Sol,” “GPT-6 Astra,” and “Claude Opus” desktop apps. The attackers bundled malware with genuine signed executables, without compromising OpenAI or Anthropic.

The attackers promoted the fake apps through GitHub project pages, including GitHub.io, that described their features and linked to ZIP downloads hosted on GitHub releases. Keeping both the promotional pages and downloads on a familiar platform helped the offers look credible to people searching for AI software.

Some of these pages appeared among the top Google results. Check Point found no signs of artificially inflated GitHub stars or forks, but said the wording and search visibility suggested the attackers had optimised the pages to attract users through Google.

Anyone who downloaded and ran the package would launch a genuine, signed application executable. The attackers had placed a malicious file called winmm.dll beside it, which the application then loaded through a technique called DLL sideloading. Although the executable’s signature was valid, the file it loaded contained the malware.

Malware Demands Administrator Access

The malicious DLL, named YobaDropper by researchers, checks its execution environment before proceeding. Without administrator privileges, it displays a message requesting elevated access and exits.

It also excludes several keyboard languages, including Russian and Belarusian, while Ukrainian remains eligible. Keyboard settings are a filtering mechanism, however, and do not reliably identify a user’s location.

After installation, a scheduled task launches a copied Windows executable three minutes after startup. That program loads YobaLoader, allowing the infection to survive a restart.

A Telegram Image Helps Locate the Next Payload

According to Check Point’s detailed technical research, YobaLoader downloads a Telegram channel’s profile image and uses its final 50 bytes to generate a domain name. Changing the image lets the operator change that destination.

The loader then queries Google’s DNS-over-HTTPS service for instructions stored in a DNS TXT record. It verifies and decrypts those instructions before retrieving an encrypted payload, with Catbox used in the examined delivery chain.

Researchers observed XMRig cryptocurrency-mining software communicating through Tor. It can pause while someone uses the computer, reducing the chance that noticeable resource consumption alerts them. The loader also supports Windows executable and PowerShell payloads, so its capabilities are not limited to mining.

Signed Files Do Not Make an Unofficial Installer Safe

Check Point advises obtaining AI tools from verified sources and restricting execution of applications from unknown publishers or repositories. A familiar product name, a GitHub download page and a signed executable can all appear inside the same malicious package.

The campaign targets people choosing where to download AI tools. Checking that source before installation, particularly before granting administrator access, is the practical step users can take to avoid these counterfeit applications.

Waqas
I am a UK-based cybersecurity journalist with a passion for covering the latest happenings in cybersecurity and tech world. I am also into gaming, reading and investigative journalism.

item.title: Beyond Cold Storage: Why Hardware Wallets Need Open Source and Clear Signing
item.description:
For years, hardware wallets have been treated as the gold standard for protecting cryptocurrency. By keeping private keys off internet-connected devices, they shut out a whole class of threats, from malware to phishing. But recent attacks have exposed a gap in that model: a well-protected key offers little defense if the person using it can’t tell what they are signing.

The Bybit hack in February 2025 made that painfully clear. North Korea’s Lazarus Group compromised a developer’s machine at Safe{Wallet}, the multisig platform Bybit used to manage its Ethereum cold wallet, and injected malicious code into the signing interface.

Bybit’s signers saw what looked like a routine transfer. What their hardware wallets actually signed was a change to the wallet’s underlying logic that handed control to the attackers. Roughly $1.5 billion in ETH was stolen, the largest crypto theft on record at the time.

The keys were never extracted. The devices did exactly what they were designed to do. That raises an uncomfortable question for the industry: how much protection does cold storage provide if users can’t independently verify what they authorize?

As smart-contract wallets, multisig accounts and complex onchain operations become the norm, the answer increasingly depends on three things working together: transparent software, inspectable hardware and transaction verification that happens on the device itself.

Why Isn’t Cold Storage Enough?

A hardware wallet’s job is simple. It generates and stores private keys on a dedicated device, away from the computer or phone that connects to the internet. When a transaction needs signing, the connected app sends the data to the device, which signs it internally and returns the signature without ever exposing the key.

That design makes it very hard for remote attackers to steal keys. It does nothing to stop a user from approving a malicious transaction. A hardware wallet can keep a key perfectly isolated while still signing a transaction that drains funds, changes account permissions or grants a malicious contract access to assets.

Blind signing is when a hardware wallet asks a user to approve a transaction it can’t display in readable form, showing raw contract data or incomplete details instead of a clear account of what the transaction will do. When the screen on the connected computer is also compromised, as it was at Bybit, the signer has no trustworthy view of the transaction anywhere.

Bybit was not an isolated case. In October 2024, attackers drained roughly $50 million from lending protocol Radiant Capital using a similar playbook. Malware on three developers’ devices showed legitimate-looking transactions in the Safe interface, while the hardware wallets were signing a transfer of contract ownership. Each signer approved what they believed was routine.

None of this means hardware wallets are ineffective. It means offline key storage is only half the job. For anyone managing large holdings, multisig accounts or DAO treasuries, the other half, verifying intent, matters just as much.

Why Open Source Matters

There is also the question of what runs inside the device. Most users have no visibility into how their hardware wallet works. They rely on the manufacturer to write secure firmware, generate keys properly and make sure the physical components behave as advertised.

Open-source development replaces some of that trust with inspection. When firmware is public, independent researchers can review the code, find vulnerabilities and propose fixes. Open-source hardware extends the same idea to circuit-board designs and component layouts, and in some cases lets technically capable users build their own devices.

Transparency is not the same as security, however. Open code can still contain bugs, and public hardware designs do nothing to stop a tampered component from entering the supply chain. Independent audits, secure manufacturing and ongoing maintenance remain essential.

Publishing code also isn’t the same as making a device verifiable. Reproducible builds close part of that gap by letting anyone compile the firmware from source and confirm the result matches the binary the manufacturer ships. The goal is security that can be examined and tested, not security users are asked to take on faith.

What Makes a Hardware Wallet Trustworthy?

No single feature does it. A trustworthy device combines several layers.

Secure key generation and storage. Keys should be created in a protected environment and never leave it. Secure elements add hardware-level resistance to physical extraction attacks, but a secure element on its own guarantees little. How it is implemented, and how it interacts with the surrounding hardware and firmware, matters just as much.

Firmware transparency. Firmware governs how the device handles keys, processes transactions and communicates with other devices. If it can’t be inspected, users have to trust the manufacturer. Public source code helps most when it comes with documented build and verification procedures.

Transaction verification. This is the most overlooked requirement. A device should do more than confirm it received a transaction; it should show what the transaction will do, including transfers, token approvals, contract calls and changes to account permissions.

Supply-chain integrity. Even a well-designed device can be compromised before it reaches the user, through swapped components or tampering during manufacturing. Inspectable hardware and manufacturing controls belong in the same conversation as firmware security.

What Is Clear Signing?

Simple transfers are easy to display: a recipient and an amount. Smart-contract interactions are not. A single transaction can bundle token approvals, transfers, contract calls and ownership changes, and multisig wallets routinely batch several operations together. Raw calldata means little to most users, and even experienced developers struggle to read it without context.

Clear signing is the alternative: the hardware wallet decodes the transaction and shows, in plain language on its own screen, what it will actually do. Where that translation happens is the crucial part. If the computer or browser is compromised, nothing it displays can be trusted. The hardware wallet has to interpret the transaction independently and present its own account of what will happen.

The industry is starting to standardize this. ERC-7730, a format first proposed by Ledger and now stewarded by the Ethereum Foundation, lets developers describe how their contracts’ functions should be displayed, so any compatible wallet can show the same readable summary instead of raw data. The more wallets and applications adopt a shared format, the less clear signing depends on any single vendor.

On-device decoding won’t stop every attack, particularly ones involving unfamiliar contracts or malicious application logic. But it gives signers a real chance to catch something suspicious before they approve it, which is exactly what Bybit’s signers lacked.

Ambire Ice: One Approach in Practice

These ideas are already shaping new hardware. On October 30, self-custodial wallet developer Ambire unveiled Ambire Ice, an open-source hardware wallet built for Ambire and Safe smart accounts. It joins a small but growing group of open-source signers, including Trezor and Keystone, whose firmware outsiders can inspect.

Rather than pitching Ice primarily as offline key storage, Ambire has centered the design on transaction verification. The device reconstructs Safe transactions itself and displays each action on its screen, so signers can review transfers, token approvals and batched operations before approving them. It also warns when a transaction would change a Safe’s owners, signature threshold or modules. According to Ambire, it blocks DELEGATECALLs to unknown contracts unless they appear on an allowlist, which targets the type of call used in the Bybit attack.

On the hardware side, Ice pairs secure elements from NXP and Infineon to guard against different kinds of physical attacks. A physical switch disconnects USB data and cuts power to Bluetooth, enabling fully offline signing through animated QR codes, while USB and Bluetooth remain available for those who want them. The firmware is a fork of Trezor’s open-source codebase; Ambire says the hardware designs and board files are open to inspection, and a transparent enclosure lets users see the internal components for themselves.

Taken together, the design reflects a broader shift: pairing isolated key storage with transaction-level verification and a hardware and software stack that outsiders can check. None of these features makes a device immune to attack, and Ambire’s claims will still need independent testing. Their value lies in giving researchers and users more to inspect and verify.

Self-Custody Is About More Than Private Keys

The crypto industry has spent years teaching users to protect their seed phrases and keep their keys offline. That advice still holds, but the complexity of today’s onchain activity has opened a new gap. A hardware wallet that guards keys but can’t clearly communicate what a user is authorizing leaves the most consequential step, the decision to sign, resting on trust.

Open-source firmware, inspectable hardware, sound key generation and on-device transaction decoding each address part of that gap. None is sufficient alone. Together, they make a device’s security assumptions easier to examine and challenge.

The goal is no longer just to keep private keys offline. It is to give users good reason to trust what happens when they press “sign.”

(Photo by Mariia Berezovsky on Unsplash)

item.title: OpenMatter Network Positions Decentralized Computing as an Alternative to Data Centers for AI
item.description:
Melbourne, Florida, November 5th, 2026, CyberNewswire

OpenMatter Network, a pioneer in decentralized infrastructure for agentic artificial intelligence, is positioning its decentralized computing platform as an alternative to massive, centralized data center development amid growing public opposition to new facilities. The company says its approach can support continued AI adoption by enabling computing workloads to run across distributed resources rather than relying primarily on large-scale data center infrastructure.

The results of Tuesday’s midterm elections have put growing public opposition to massive data center development in the national spotlight. However, according to OpenMatter Network, resistance to new facilities need not signal a slowdown in AI adoption. Instead, it could accelerate the transition to a computing model that reduces dependence on massive, centralized data centers.

“Voters have made it clear that they are increasingly concerned about the enormous energy demands, environmental impact and rising utility costs associated with massive data center development,” said Mike Anderson, CEO of OpenMatter Network. “But the need to deploy agentic AI isn’t going away. Businesses don’t have to choose between advancing AI and addressing these very legitimate concerns. There is another path forward, and OpenMatter is helping make it possible.”

Across the country, communities have expressed concerns about the impact of large-scale facilities on electricity rates, water supplies, local infrastructure and the environment. The election has brought renewed attention to those concerns and the policy choices surrounding new construction.

“The assumption that AI must be built around increasingly massive concentrations of computing power deserves to be challenged,” Anderson continued. “Our decentralized architecture allows computing resources to be distributed across many different locations. That means organizations have another way to move forward with agentic AI as communities and policymakers reconsider the costs and consequences of building more enormous data centers.”

The OpenMatter Network platform is designed to transform widely available computing hardware into usable network resources through its distributed architecture, algorithms and verifiable computing capabilities. By enabling independently owned computing resources to participate in a shared network, OpenMatter is working to make decentralized infrastructure a practical alternative for enterprise AI deployment.

“There’s an enormous amount of computing capacity outside the walls of traditional data centers,” said Renee Davis, co-founder and chief business officer of OpenMatter Network. “Our technology makes it possible to bring those resources together in a verifiable network capable of supporting real-world AI workloads. Rather than concentrating computing power in a relatively small number of massive facilities, we can distribute workloads across existing resources and smaller installations, creating opportunities for a more flexible and potentially more energy-efficient approach to AI infrastructure.”

The decentralized model also offers organizations greater flexibility in where computing resources are located and how they are deployed. This can be particularly valuable for businesses and government institutions seeking greater control over computing infrastructure, including those with requirements for data sovereignty and locally managed resources.

“The question is no longer simply how many more massive data centers we need to build,” Anderson concluded. “It’s how we can deploy the AI capabilities businesses need without imposing unnecessary burdens on the communities where computing resources are located. Tuesday’s election results make that question more urgent than ever. OpenMatter offers a new way forward.”

About OpenMatter Network

Headquartered in Florida’s Space Coast, OpenMatter Network is building the Verifiable Trust Layer for Secure Collaboration and AI Agents. Guided by the principle “Don’t Trust Data. Prove It.,” the company’s cryptographically verifiable architecture enables secure collaboration, governed AI behavior and mathematically verifiable execution across untrusted environments. For more information, visit www.openmatter.network.

item.title: Hackers Tamper With Refrigeration Controls at France’s National Blood Service
item.description:
Hackers changed refrigeration controls at three sites operated by France’s national blood service, prompting staff to secure stored plasma and move supplies before any products were damaged.

The Établissement français du sang (EFS) said the November 2 incident affected equipment managed through a refrigeration supplier, with no interruption to blood collection or distribution.

The incident follows attacks on supermarket and food-supplier refrigeration systems in Europe. At the EFS facilities, however, the affected cold rooms held plasma intended for transfusions and the manufacture of medicines, along with stored biological samples.

In its November 3 statement, EFS said temperature and defrost thresholds had been changed to extremely high settings. Its monitoring and alarm systems detected the changes, allowing staff to intervene before the stored products were affected.

“No health consequences have been identified, and no blood products were lost,” the organisation said.

Staff Intervened Before Plasma Was Damaged

According to Le Canard enchaîné, whose reporting was also covered by TF1, the attack occurred overnight from November 1 to 2. Settings on equipment normally maintained around minus 30°C were reportedly changed to 110°C.

That figure describes a programmed setting, not a temperature the plasma reached. EFS confirmed that operating thresholds had been altered but did not publish the 110°C figure itself.

An on-duty technician reportedly noticed the problem during the night. Depending on the installation, staff brought the equipment under control or took it out of service and transferred products to other cold-storage facilities.

EFS said neither the plasma nor its stored samples were damaged. The organisation has strengthened equipment and temperature monitoring while its technical teams work with France’s national cybersecurity agency, ANSSI, and the Health Ministry.

Investigators are examining how the hackers gained access, which equipment was affected and the conditions required to return installations to service safely.

Supplier Points to a Third-Party Component

Although EFS did not identify its refrigeration supplier in its statement, Le Canard enchaîné named Coolworld, including in connection with facilities in Bourgogne-Franche-Comté.

Coolworld subsequently acknowledged a cybersecurity incident involving refrigeration remote-monitoring software. In its November 4 statement, the company said a limited number of its units had been affected and attributed the vulnerability described in media reports to a third-party component outside its direct control.

The company said it had taken protective measures and was supporting customers where needed, but declined to discuss individual cases. Its statement did not identify the component or explain how the hackers accessed the affected systems.

Similar Attacks Have Disrupted Food Businesses

The EFS incident follows attacks on refrigeration systems at European supermarkets and UK food suppliers. Those incidents involved altered temperature settings, defrost functions and, in some cases, disabled alerts. Several retailers had to discard food.

French supermarkets experienced similar disruption in October. Investigators have not established whether the EFS incident involved the same hackers or access method.

For healthcare facilities, independent alarms and staff intervention can determine whether tampering becomes a loss of medical supplies. At EFS, both allowed employees to act before the products were damaged.

Darin Fredde, Senior Director of Technical Marketing Engineering at Ridge Security, highlighted that distinction in comments shared with Hackread.com.

“There’s also an important distinction between changing a temperature setpoint and changing the physical temperature. We shouldn’t confuse an attempted manipulation with a confirmed physical consequence. Fortunately, the reported monitoring, alarms, and staff response appear to have prevented damage.”

Damon Small, a board member at Xcape, Inc., said access to equipment affecting human safety requires strict controls.

“Any device capable of affecting human safety that is connected to the Internet must have strong authentication and access controls. Access should be restricted to authorized users through appropriate filtering and security mechanisms. These systems deserve the same level of protection as any other critical operational technology.”

Deeba Ahmed
Deeba is a veteran cybersecurity reporter at Hackread.com with over a decade of experience covering cybercrime, vulnerabilities, and security events. Her expertise and in-depth analysis make her a key contributor to the platform’s trusted coverage.

item.title: How Governments Detect VPN Traffic, and Why Encryption Alone Doesn’t Hide It
item.description:
A VPN that works perfectly at home can stop working the moment its user lands in a country with a national firewall. The encryption hasn’t changed. Nobody has broken AES or cracked a WireGuard key. The tunnel is just as secure as it was the day before, and it still gets blocked within minutes.

That’s because a VPN hides what you send, not that you’re using a VPN. Censors don’t need to read your traffic to stop it. They read everything around it: the handshake that opens the connection, the size and timing of packets, the reputation of the server’s IP address, and how that server responds when someone else knocks on its door. Detecting VPN traffic is a contest over signals, not encryption strength, and the people building national firewalls have become very good at reading those signals.

The detection stack, from cheap to expensive

Network operators don’t rely on a single technique. They layer methods, usually starting with the cheapest and adding more expensive ones as their budget and motivation allow.

  • IP reputation and blocklists. The simplest approach is to block the addresses VPN servers live on. Commercial VPNs run thousands of servers, but they sit in known datacenter ranges, and IP intelligence databases track which addresses belong to which providers. Streaming services and banking sites rely on this layer too, which is why a VPN can be “detected” by a website that never inspects a single packet.
  • Port and protocol blocking. Many networks simply drop traffic on ports they don’t expect, or block UDP outright. OpenVPN defaults to UDP port 1194, and WireGuard has no mandatory port and uses UDP. Some providers carry its traffic inside an additional transport to get through network restrictions. Moving a VPN to TCP port 443, the port used by HTTPS, gets past a basic port filter. It isn’t a disguise, though. Port 443 tells a firewall where the traffic is going, not what it is.
  • Deep packet inspection (DPI). DPI looks at the structure of the traffic, and the major VPN protocols are easy to recognize. WireGuard’s handshake uses fixed message types and sizes: the initiation message is always 148 bytes and the response is always 92. OpenVPN leaves telltale patterns in its packet headers.
  • In a USENIX Security 2022 paper, researchers combined passive traffic analysis with active probing. Working with an ISP serving about a million users, they identified more than 85% of OpenVPN flows with negligible false positives. Their method also identified connections using 34 of the 41 obfuscated VPN configurations tested.
  • TLS fingerprinting. Plenty of circumvention tools wrap their traffic in TLS so it looks like ordinary HTTPS. But the TLS handshake carries its own fingerprint: the cipher suites offered, the extensions requested and the order they appear in. A Chrome browser, a Python script and a VPN client all build that handshake differently. A firewall that expects to see browsers and sees something else has a reason to look harder.

Active probing requires the censor to make additional connections to suspected servers and examine their responses. When a censor suspects a server is a proxy, it connects to that server itself and sends test traffic to see how it reacts.

A real web server answers like a web server. A poorly built proxy might hang, reset the connection or respond in a way no normal website would. China’s Great Firewall has used active probing for years to discover hidden Tor bridges and Shadowsocks servers.

Each layer looks for a different clue, which is why fixing one problem rarely fixes the whole thing. Moving to port 443 beats a port filter but not DPI, and a clean IP address beats a blocklist but not a protocol fingerprint.

For a practical explanation of options such as changing ports and enabling obfuscation, this guide to making your VPN harder to detect discusses common approaches. Their effectiveness depends on how the network identifies and blocks connections.

For years, the standard advice for beating DPI was to make traffic look like nothing at all. Protocols like Shadowsocks, VMess and obfs4 encrypt every byte, including the handshake, so the stream looks like uniform random noise with no headers or fingerprints to match.

In November 2021, China’s Great Firewall turned that idea on its head. A USENIX Security 2023 study of how the Great Firewall detects and blocks fully encrypted traffic found that the censor had stopped trying to identify those protocols directly. Instead, it used simple, cheap rules to exempt traffic that was unlikely to be fully encrypted, and treated everything else as suspect.

The system allowed traffic that resembled recognised protocols such as TLS or HTTP, or met other exemption rules. Those rules examined the proportion of set bits and the number and position of printable ASCII characters in the first TCP data packet. Connections that did not qualify for an exemption could trigger blocking.

During their measurements, the researchers observed blocking focused on selected hosting-provider IP ranges, with a roughly 26% probability of a qualifying connection triggering it. Separately, applying the inferred detection rules to university network traffic would have classified about 0.6% of TCP connections for blocking. That simulation did not apply the firewall’s restrictions on destination ranges or sampling.

The lesson for anyone designing or relying on circumvention tools is uncomfortable. Randomness is itself a signal. On an internet where almost everything starts with a recognizable handshake, a connection that starts with nothing stands out.

How circumvention tools adapted

The response has been to stop looking like nothing and start looking like something ordinary.

  • TLS mimicry. Many VPN providers now offer “stealth” or obfuscated protocols that wrap the tunnel inside traffic built to resemble a normal HTTPS session. Proton VPN’s Stealth protocol, launched in October 2022, uses obfuscated TLS tunneling over TCP, and Proton says it is more censorship-resistant than simply running a VPN over port 443, because DPI can still recognize a VPN handshake on any port. Some newer tools go further and borrow the TLS identity of a real, popular website, so that even an active probe gets a legitimate-looking reply.
  • Wrapping WireGuard instead of replacing it. WireGuard is fast and well audited, but its fixed handshake makes it easy to spot. Rather than abandon it, providers wrap it inside other transports. Mullvad, which shut down OpenVPN support on January 15, 2026, now relies on anti-censorship methods that carry WireGuard over other protocols, including QUIC and Shadowsocks, so the network sees the wrapper rather than the WireGuard handshake underneath.
  • Rethinking older obfuscation. The 2021 findings changed the calculation for plain Shadowsocks in particular. It is still useful on networks that only filter ports or match protocol signatures, but on a network running the Great Firewall’s entropy rules. These findings show why plain Shadowsocks can be blocked even without a conventional protocol signature. TLS mimicry offers another approach, but its effectiveness depends on the implementation and the network’s detection rules.

None of these approaches is permanent. Each one removes a signal the censor currently relies on, and each invites the censor to find a new one.

The same playbook runs on corporate and campus networks

National firewalls get the headlines, but scaled-down versions of the same stack run on office and university networks every day. Next-generation firewalls identify applications by behavior rather than port, flag known VPN protocols with DPI, and block datacenter IP ranges on guest Wi-Fi.

For security teams, that cuts both ways. The visibility that lets a firewall spot an unsanctioned VPN also exposes how much a network can infer about encrypted traffic without decrypting it. For users, it means “the VPN connected” doesn’t mean “the VPN went unnoticed.” A connection can be allowed through and still be logged as VPN traffic.

The legal and practical reality

Some countries restrict or ban VPN use, and in those places hiding a VPN can carry legal consequences that go well beyond losing a connection. On corporate and school networks, bypassing controls can break acceptable-use policies even where it breaks no law.

Practically, well-funded censors update their rules continuously. A setup that works this week may fail the next, and the more resources a network operator puts into detection, the shorter that window becomes.

Conclusion

VPN detection isn’t about breaking encryption. It’s about reading everything encryption leaves exposed: addresses, ports, handshakes, entropy and behavior under probing. The Great Firewall’s move against fully encrypted traffic showed how a censor can turn a protocol’s greatest strength into its weakness with a few cheap heuristics.

The tools that survive in this environment are the ones that blend in with ordinary traffic rather than hiding from it. As long as censors keep adding signals and tool builders keep removing them, the arms race will continue, and it will be fought over metadata, not math.

A VPN can protect the contents of a connection while leaving enough visible information for a network to identify or block it. Obfuscation can reduce some of those signals, but a successful connection does not prove that VPN use went undetected.

item.title: CISA Warns Hackers Are Exploiting 18-Year-Old WordPress Core Vulnerability
item.description:
CVE-2026-119977 lets hackers hijack WordPress sites during core updates. CISA confirms exploitation as users are told to patch and protect upgrades.

The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has warned that attackers are exploiting a WordPress core vulnerability that can let them take over websites during an update. Tracked as CVE-2026-119977, the vulnerability affects the updater’s handling of temporary installation files and can allow remote code execution without an account on the targeted site.

The vulnerability was found by Umut Bayram, a security researcher at Picus Security. It carries a CVSS score of 8.1 and was added to CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on November 3.

Although the disclosure is recent, Bayram traced the underlying behaviour to WordPress 2.7, released in 2008. Public advisories list affected versions from 4.7 through 7.1.3, while his research describes older releases as affected too. Whether an installation can be exploited depends on its update package, server configuration and the attacker’s ability to locate the temporary files.

How an Update Can Expose a Website

During a core update, WordPress extracts downloaded files into a temporary directory under wp-content/upgrade/ before copying them into the live installation. If the package contains the WordPress installer and the server allows web access and PHP execution in that directory, an attacker can reach a temporary copy of WordPress while the update is running.

The temporary installer checks nearby locations for an existing configuration file but does not find the live site’s wp-config.php. It therefore treats the extracted copy as an installation that has not yet been configured.

An attacker who reaches it in time can supply connection details for a database they control. The installer then creates a new wp-config.php inside the temporary directory.

On vulnerable releases, the updater can copy that attacker-created file over the live site’s configuration. This redirects WordPress to the attacker’s database, where they can create an administrator account. On a typical single-site installation that permits administrators to install plugins, this provides a route to executing PHP code on the server.

Bayram describes the sequence in his published technical analysis. The attack depends on winning a time-of-check time-of-use race condition, meaning the attacker must act between stages of the update before WordPress removes the temporary installation.

Not every update exposes the necessary files. The attacker also needs to determine the staging directory’s location. Some older releases added randomness to that path, making exploitation dependent on another way to learn its name.

WordPress Has Released Fixes

WordPress released version 7.1.4 on October 28 to address the vulnerability. The fix randomises temporary directory names, preserves a file that prevents directory listings and stops a staged wp-config.php from being copied over the live configuration.

Security fixes were also backported to older branches down to 4.7. WordPress notes that only its latest version is actively supported. Releases from 2.7 through 4.6 did not receive this fix and should be upgraded.

For applicable federal systems, CISA set November 6 as the remediation deadline and listed forensic triage as required under Binding Operational Directive 26-04. Its exploitation warning does not identify the attackers or disclose how many websites have been compromised.

The First Patched Update Still Needs Protection

Installing the fix requires an additional precaution because the extraction stage runs through the updater already installed on the website.

When an unpatched site updates to a fixed release, the new code prevents the temporary configuration file from replacing the live one. However, the old extraction code can still leave a temporary installer at a predictable, web-accessible location.

An attacker could configure that temporary installation and execute PHP code before WordPress cleans it up. Code running there would have the web server’s permissions, including whatever access those permissions provide to the live site’s files.

Bayram recommends denying web access to wp-content/upgrade/ before starting the update and confirming that requests to the directory return a 403 response. The restriction should be applied through the server configuration or the WordPress root .htaccess file, not inside the upgrade directory, where the updater could delete it.

Alternatively, administrators can download and extract the patched release outside the public web directory, then manually replace the core files while preserving wp-config.php and wp-content. A standard wp core update command is not a substitute for that method because it uses the same core updater.

Research Took About Four Hours With AI Assistance

Bayram said he found the vulnerability using GPT-5.6 Sol as a research partner, taking about four hours from examining the updater to producing a working exploit chain.

In comments shared with Hackread.com, he warned that faster vulnerability research also gives attackers more opportunities to find weaknesses in widely deployed software.

“If an early-career researcher can find a two-decade-old RCE in an afternoon, so can an attacker,” Bayram said.

He also noted that production updates take time, leaving organisations exposed even after a patch becomes available.

“Until then, there’s a window where you’re exposed, and that’s exactly where attackers are working,” he said.

Bayram urged organisations to validate their defences when systems change, rather than waiting for scheduled testing.

“That’s the signal, and that’s when you need to find out whether you’re exploitable and whether your controls would actually stop it.”

If the package contains the WordPress installer and the server allows web access and PHP execution in that directory, an attacker can reach a temporary copy of WordPress while the update is running.

The temporary installer checks nearby locations for an existing configuration file but does not find the live site’s wp-config.php. It therefore treats the extracted copy as an installation that has not yet been configured.

An attacker who reaches it in time can supply connection details for a database they control. The installer then creates a new wp-config.php inside the temporary directory.

On vulnerable releases, the updater can copy that attacker-created file over the live site’s configuration. This redirects WordPress to the attacker’s database, where they can create an administrator account. On a typical single-site installation that permits administrators to install plugins, this provides a route to executing PHP code on the server.

Bayram describes the sequence in his published technical analysis. The attack depends on winning a time-of-check time-of-use race condition, meaning the attacker must act between stages of the update before WordPress removes the temporary installation.

Not every update exposes the necessary files. The attacker also needs to determine the staging directory’s location. Some older releases added randomness to that path, making exploitation dependent on another way to learn its name.

WordPress Has Released Fixes

WordPress released version 7.1.4 on October 28 to address the vulnerability. The fix randomises temporary directory names, preserves a file that prevents directory listings and stops a staged wp-config.php from being copied over the live configuration.

Security fixes were also backported to older branches down to 4.7. WordPress notes that only its latest version is actively supported. Releases from 2.7 through 4.6 did not receive this fix and should be upgraded.

For applicable federal systems, CISA set November 6 as the remediation deadline and listed forensic triage as required under Binding Operational Directive 26-04. Its exploitation warning does not identify the attackers or disclose how many websites have been compromised.

The First Patched Update Still Needs Protection

Installing the fix requires an additional precaution because the extraction stage runs through the updater already installed on the website.

When an unpatched site updates to a fixed release, the new code prevents the temporary configuration file from replacing the live one. However, the old extraction code can still leave a temporary installer at a predictable, web-accessible location.

An attacker could configure that temporary installation and execute PHP code before WordPress cleans it up. Code running there would have the web server’s permissions, including whatever access those permissions provide to the live site’s files.

Bayram recommends denying web access to wp-content/upgrade/ before starting the update and confirming that requests to the directory return a 403 response. The restriction should be applied through the server configuration or the WordPress root .htaccess file, not inside the upgrade directory, where the updater could delete it.

Alternatively, administrators can download and extract the patched release outside the public web directory, then manually replace the core files while preserving wp-config.php and wp-content. A standard wp core update command is not a substitute for that method because it uses the same core updater.

Research Took About Four Hours With AI Assistance

Bayram said he found the vulnerability using GPT-5.6 Sol as a research partner, taking about four hours from examining the updater to producing a working exploit chain.

In comments shared with Hackread.com, he warned that faster vulnerability research also gives attackers more opportunities to find weaknesses in widely deployed software.

“If an early-career researcher can find a two-decade-old RCE in an afternoon, so can an attacker,” Bayram said.

He also noted that production updates take time, leaving organisations exposed even after a patch becomes available.

“Until then, there’s a window where you’re exposed, and that’s exactly where attackers are working,” he said.

Bayram urged organisations to validate their defences when systems change, rather than waiting for scheduled testing.

“That’s the signal, and that’s when you need to find out whether you’re exploitable and whether your controls would actually stop it.”

item.title: Insignary Releases Free Insignary-Chk Tool to Detect PHP2Shell and Node2Shell Exposure
item.description:
Toronto, Canada, November 6th, 2026, CyberNewswire

Free, read-only scanner helps organizations find Linux servers and container images exposed to two actively exploited vulnerabilities in PHP and Node.js

Insignary, a global open-source security company, today released insignary-chk, a free tool that checks for PHP2Shell and Node2Shell, two recently disclosed runtime vulnerabilities affecting PHP and Node.js.

PHP2Shell refers to two vulnerabilities in the PHP runtime (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619), each rated 9.2 (Critical) under CVSS v4.0, that can allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute code remotely. Servers that handle web requests with PHP are at risk, including deployments using Apache mod_php, PHP-FPM, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed. The PHP Project released fixes on October 21, 2026, in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35. PHP 8.1 and earlier have reached end of life and no longer receive official releases. Because the flaws sit in the runtime itself rather than in application code, code review alone cannot reveal them, so organizations also need to find PHP instances bundled inside vendor software and container images.

Node2Shell (CVE-2026-111497) is an out-of-bounds write flaw in Google’s Brotli decompression library, which Node.js bundles. Specially crafted compressed data can crash an affected application, expose its memory, or allow remote code execution. The issue is fixed in Node.js 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1. Node.js’s official end-of-life policy treats any unsupported branch (e.g., 20.x and earlier) as carrying ongoing risk once support ends, since no further security fixes are issued. insignary-chk reflects this by design: it does not flag EOL branches like Node.js 20.x as “Likely vulnerable”; instead, it surfaces them as “Check with OS vendor” when installed from a Linux distribution package, or “Unable to determine” when installed from nodejs.org or built from source, so administrators can verify the actual patch status with their vendor or upgrade to a supported release. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has added both PHP2Shell and Node2Shell to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

insignary-chk is a single file that requires no installation or registration. It is read-only by default: it only reads files, never runs what it finds, and makes no changes unless the user chooses the –fix option. It sends no data over the network, except when the user chooses an option that connects to an address they specify. Because Node2Shell originates in the Brotli library, insignary-chk also checks Brotli copies outside Node.js, including the system Brotli library and Python’s brotli package. End-of-life PHP versions are likewise flagged for review against the Linux distribution’s security advisory, or for upgrade to a supported release. Results are ranked by priority, so teams can see at a glance which issues need urgent attention.

The report’s to-do list is sorted by urgency: “Act now” for vulnerable files in use by a running process, “Fix soon” for vulnerable software that is installed but not running, and “Review” for items that need a manual check, followed by detailed findings for each server or container image.

insignary-chk complements the Insignary Clarity product family. Insignary Clarity uses the company’s patented binary software composition analysis (SCA) to identify components and versions inside compiled applications, firmware, IT infrastructure, and container images, without requiring source code. Insignary Clarity SC brings results from Clarity, Clarity AIR, third-party SCA tools, and imported SBOMs (software bills of materials) into one platform, and maps newly disclosed CVEs to existing SBOMs without rescanning. Users who already run Clarity can use insignary-chk’s –clarity option to confirm its findings with binary analysis on their own Clarity server.

“PHP2Shell and Node2Shell sit in the runtime, not in application code, so reviewing source code alone won’t show whether you’re exposed,” said Taek Wan Kim, President & CEO of Insignary. “We built insignary-chk so any organization can check its Linux servers and containers within minutes, without making changes to its systems, and focus first on the issues that matter most.”

insignary-chk is available as a free download, with no sign-up required, at www.insignary.com/free-tools/php2shell-node2shell-checker. It runs on Linux x86_64 and checks only the three CVEs listed above. Windows, macOS, and arm64 are not yet supported.

About Insignary

Insignary Inc. is a Toronto-based cybersecurity company specializing in binary composition analysis and software supply chain security. Its patented technology enables organizations to identify open-source software components, vulnerabilities, and software provenance directly from compiled binaries without requiring access to source code. The company serves enterprises, governments, and software vendors worldwide and is backed by strategic investors and partners including BearingPoint in Europe, Cybertrust Japan and TechMatrix in Japan, and TMA Solutions. Through its global partner ecosystem, Insignary supports software supply chain security initiatives across North America, Europe, and Asia. For more information, visit www.insignary.com.

Jessica Lee

item.title: Railway Engineer Admits Running AI Agents Against Rival Cloud Platform
item.description:
A Railway engineer admitted testing AI agents on Primcloud, whose founder says they sought customer secrets and scanned its network.

An engineer at cloud platform Railway has acknowledged running AI agents against competing cloud platform Primcloud after its founder reported attempts to obtain customer secrets and scan internal systems. Primcloud says its controls blocked the attempts and no customer data was accessed.

Josh Manders, Primcloud’s founder, publicly challenged Railway on November 3, identifying senior product engineer Jake Runzer as the person behind the activity. Runzer accepted responsibility for running the agents, describing their purpose as signups and automated testing on similar platforms.

Railway co-founder and CEO Jake Cooper initially apologised. In a later statement, he said the employee built and operated the tool personally outside work hours and that Railway took internal action.

His explanation adds an important distinction to the dispute, which concerns an employee’s acknowledged activity, not evidence of a company-directed operation against a competitor.

Primcloud Describes Attempts to Reach Other Customers’ Secrets

According to Manders’ account, the activity went considerably further than trying the platform’s signup process. He said credentials available inside the account’s application container were used to request platform secrets, including those belonging to other customers.

The agents also attempted to reach the cloud provider’s metadata endpoint, checked what the container credentials could access and searched for databases and caches by guessing internal names, Manders said. Cloud metadata services can expose temporary credentials when accessible without adequate restrictions.

Manders described roughly 24 commands over 15 minutes, including two scans covering 65,536 internal network addresses. That is his reported address count, not a count of confirmed live hosts or exposed services. He said no application was run and the attempts to reach protected resources were blocked.

These technical details remain Primcloud’s account of the activity. Runzer acknowledged operating the agents, but that acknowledgement does not independently verify every command, target or outcome Manders described.

Railway Says the Tool Was a Personal Project

In his reply to Manders, Runzer said he had been running agents for signups and testing on similar platforms. He denied malicious intent and said he had stopped the system after recognising that it was reaching too far.

Cooper’s later statement described a personal tool intended to identify and report bugs through bounty programmes. He said the employee used personal accounts, a personal credit card and a subscription to a hosted service running DeepSeek.

According to Cooper, the tool ran once against one external provider and was stopped within 15 minutes. He said Railway did not condone the conduct and had addressed it with the employee, without specifying what action had been taken. He also distinguished the activity from Railway’s authorised internal security testing.

The description of the tool as a bug-bounty project does not establish that Primcloud authorised the testing. Nor do the public statements establish why the agents selected each action or how closely a person supervised their execution.

Responsibility Remains With the Operator

For the company receiving the requests, the immediate concern is what the software does inside its environment. Ram Varadarajan, CEO of Acalvio, said in comments shared with Hackread.com that distinguishing an agent’s intentions is an unreliable basis for protection.

“Whether you call it a rogue agent or agentic testing, the defender sees the same behavior: something inside the environment is harvesting credentials and mapping the network. Unfortunately, you can’t reliably classify AI intent, especially with autonomous agents.”

Varadarajan said decoy credentials and fake internal assets can help identify activity that legitimate workflows should not trigger, regardless of whether a person or an agent initiates it.

Diana Kelley, Chief Information Security Officer at Noma Security, said organisations remain responsible for addressing actions taken by agents operating under their authority. That includes investigating incidents, notifying affected organisations and putting controls in place to prevent a recurrence.

“An agent can act without a person directing every step. It doesn’t remove the responsibility of the people and organizations that deploy it.”

Railway Disclosed Its Own Breach in October

The dispute follows a separate security incident at Railway. In its October 21 disclosure, the company said an unauthorised party may have accessed encrypted customer environment variables and obtained some decrypted contents. Those variables can contain API keys, database passwords and other credentials.

Railway’s preliminary report, published the following day, described unauthorised access to internal systems and confirmed that some encrypted environment variables had been decrypted. It advised customers to rotate sensitive credentials stored before October 21.

The report put the upper estimate of workspaces with some environment variables exposed at 1.85%, approximately 100,000 workspaces. Railway said precautionary requests to revoke credentials affected a larger population, so receiving a revocation notice did not itself establish that a customer’s secrets had been compromised.

Waqas
I am a UK-based cybersecurity journalist with a passion for covering the latest happenings in cybersecurity and tech world. I am also into gaming, reading and investigative journalism.

item.title: 7 Best Vulnerability Scanning Tools for Security Teams in (2026)
item.description:
Verizon’s 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report (DBIR) puts vulnerability exploitation at the top of its initial access vectors, at 31%. Remediation went the other way. Only 26% of the flaws in CISA’s KEV (Known Exploited Vulnerabilities) catalog were fully remediated in 2025, down from 38% a year earlier, and the median time to full resolution grew from 32 days to 43.

Those figures cover organizations of every size. On a team where one or two people own security alongside infrastructure or product work, judge a scanner by how much it leaves you to do after it finishes.

Key Takeaways

  • Intruder is the strongest all-round fit here: hosted and quick to start, with external, web app and cloud coverage in one account.
  • Aikido Security and Topscan.me both put code and running systems in the same product. Aikido leans toward developers, Topscan toward the perimeter.
  • HostedScan gives you established open-source engines without running them, and Pentest-Tools.com adds hands-on exploit validation.
  • Detectify fits when most of the risk sits in web apps and subdomains, and Tenable Nessus when internal networks matter and someone can operate a scanner.

How These Tools Were Compared

“Lean” here means one to three people who own security alongside other work, often a DevOps lead, an IT manager or a CTO. Each tool was checked against four questions from that person’s point of view:

  1. Can one person start alone? Sign up, add a target and see results without an appliance or a sales call.
  2. Does it cover what faces the internet? External infrastructure and web applications, on a plan a small team would realistically buy.
  3. Does it help decide what to fix first? Some signal beyond a raw CVSS score, and enough detail to act on a finding without reproducing it from scratch.
  4. What happens after the fix? Rescans that confirm it, a status history, and a route into Jira, Slack or similar.

The facts below come from vendors’ public pricing pages and documentation as of early November 2026. None of this is a detection benchmark, so only a trial can show accuracy on your own stack. Prices depend on asset counts and change often, so they are left out.

The 7 Best Vulnerability Scanning Tools for Lean Security Teams

Where two tools came out level on those questions, the one that removes the need for another purchase (cloud, code or internal coverage) ranks higher.

1. Intruder

Intruder pitches its plans at “lean, time-strapped teams” and keeps setup short: you connect cloud accounts, add domains and IPs, and external scanning starts with no agents. The company says it runs more than 170,000 checks against internet-facing assets. Results are ordered by severity, exploitability and threat intelligence, and each one comes with remediation steps.

Paid plans add emerging threat scans, which check your estate when a new flaw goes public instead of waiting for the next scheduled run. They also add authenticated web app and API testing, daily cloud checks across AWS, Azure and Google Cloud, and integrations such as Jira and Slack.

Best for: Small teams that want external, web and cloud coverage with little setup and a clear fix order.

Trade-off: The free plan leaves out web apps and monitors only ports 80 and 443. Internal and agent-based scanning starts at the Pro plan, which goes through sales, and automated discovery of unknown assets sits in Enterprise.

2. Aikido Security

Aikido starts from the repository. Dependency scanning, static analysis and secrets detection run alongside DAST, container scanning, infrastructure-as-code and cloud misconfiguration checks in one account. Triage is its main argument for a small team: reachability analysis filters out findings that can’t be reached, the triage learns custom context from your docs, and fixes can arrive as pull requests. The free Developer plan covers two users, ten repositories, one domain and one cloud account, with no card required.

Best for: Software teams where developers fix what the scanner finds and code is the first concern.

Trade-off: Attack surface monitoring starts at the Pro plan, and licensing counts the developers covered, which suits product teams better than IT groups with few coders. AutoTriage for code findings isn’t on the free plan.

3. Topscan.me

Topscan.me publishes what its engine runs at each stage and what it deliberately leaves alone, which helps when the person buying the scanner also answers for production. Its discovery stage works from public records (certificate transparency logs and DNS) plus a single normal HTTP request to each host, so it can map a domain before anything is approved. Port checks and active templates are limited to targets you have confirmed, at a capped request rate, and nothing destructive is sent.

A finding shows its evidence: the host, the status code, the response header or certificate date behind it, and when it was checked. The next scan closes a fixed issue with a date, and one that comes back is marked as reopened. Static code and dependency analysis for GitHub and GitLab repositories sits in the same workspace. Paid plans add web application scanning and, for perimeter findings, SLA timers that start at first detection. On the free plan, one host gets a weekly scan alongside one repository and one user, and a 14-day trial of a paid plan needs no card.

Best for: Teams where a DevOps lead or CTO owns security among other things and wants the perimeter and code under one subscription.

Trade-off: There is no internal network scanning, because hosts need a public address to be scanned. Cloud integration covers AWS only, and Slack, Microsoft Teams and Jira routing isn’t on the entry-level paid plan.

4. HostedScan

HostedScan runs established engines so you don’t have to: OpenVAS, OWASP ZAP, Nuclei, Nmap and SSLyze on every plan, with Nessus on the top tier. Triage rests on CVSS and EPSS scores and a report-card grade for each target, and you can accept, remediate and track each vulnerability through its lifecycle. Attack surface mapping and unlimited team members come with every plan, and the 14-day trial needs no card. The company counts more than 5,000 MSPs and IT teams as customers, and its reporting features lean that way.

Best for: IT teams and MSPs that trust open-source engines but lack the time to run them, and need reports for auditors or clients.

Trade-off: Authenticated scans, internal network scanning, APIs and webhooks start at the Premium plan. Source code isn’t covered.

5. Pentest-Tools.com

Pentest-Tools.com comes from the pentesting side, and its catalog of 19 tools shows it: network, website, API and cloud scanners next to recon tools and exploiters. The findings view groups similar results and flags duplicates, and you can filter by target, severity, verification state or status.

Every paid plan includes unlimited rescans on network and web app assets, scan automation, unlimited team members, and integrations such as Jira and Microsoft Teams. The Exploit plan adds Sniper, an automatic CVE exploiter, which comes in handy when an engineer asks for proof that a finding is real.

Best for: A team with some offensive security experience that wants to validate findings itself.

Trade-off: The NetScan plan has only limited web and API scanning, so a team with its own web app needs AppScan or above. Internal network scanning is an optional add-on, and the range of tools takes some learning for anyone new to pentesting.

6. Detectify

Detectify concentrates on what can be reached through domains and web apps. Surface Monitoring maps subdomains from certificate transparency logs, DNS enumeration and brute-forcing, finds open ports, and runs payload-based tests that the company says come from more than 1,765 modules built by ethical hackers in its Crowdsource community. Application Scanning goes deeper, crawling single-page apps and testing behind a recorded login.

For a small team, the payload is the useful part, because the finding shows what triggered it. Subdomain takeover checks run every eight hours, and those findings close automatically once the record is fixed. Those alerts can go to Slack, Jira or Microsoft Teams. The Starter tier has no platform fee and allows up to five users.

Best for: SaaS companies whose exposure is mainly web apps, APIs and a sprawl of subdomains.

Trade-off: Surface Monitoring and Application Scanning are billed per domain and per target, in addition to any platform fee. Internal scanning starts at the Professional tier, and tiers above Starter go through a demo or sales.

7. Tenable Nessus

Nessus appears in almost every roundup of vulnerability scanning tools and is the only tool here you run yourself. It deploys on a wide range of platforms, including a Raspberry Pi, so getting it inside an internal network is straightforward. Prioritization draws on EPSS, CVSS and Tenable’s VPR, and more than 450 preconfigured templates include configuration audits against CIS benchmarks.

Nessus Professional doesn’t include web application or external attack surface scanning, which come with Nessus Expert. Check the license before planning around the free edition, too: Tenable now describes Nessus Essentials as a 30-day license limited to five IPs and strictly for non-commercial use.

Best for: Teams with internal networks to assess and someone comfortable operating a scanner.

Trade-off: You host it, schedule it and keep it updated. Results live in the scan and its reports, so assigning findings and tracking fixes usually moves to a ticket system. Tenable itself pitches Nessus Professional at consultants, pentesters and security professionals.

The Seven Side by Side

Which One to Try First

  1. Security sits with IT and cloud accounts matter: Intruder.
  2. Developers fix most of what gets found: Aikido Security or Topscan.me.
  3. You want open-source engines without the upkeep: HostedScan.

Those figures cover organizations of every size. On a team where one or two people own security alongside infrastructure or product work, judge a scanner by how much it leaves you to do after it finishes.

  • Intruder is the strongest all-round fit here: hosted and quick to start, with external, web app and cloud coverage in one account.
  • Aikido Security and Topscan.me both put code and running systems in the same product. Aikido leans toward developers, Topscan toward the perimeter.
  • HostedScan gives you established open-source engines without running them, and Pentest-Tools.com adds hands-on exploit validation.
  • Detectify fits when most of the risk sits in web apps and subdomains, and Tenable Nessus when internal networks matter and someone can operate a scanner.

How These Tools Were Compared

“Lean” here means one to three people who own security alongside other work, often a DevOps lead, an IT manager or a CTO. Each tool was checked against four questions from that person’s point of view:

  1. Can one person start alone? Sign up, add a target and see results without an appliance or a sales call.
  2. Does it cover what faces the internet? External infrastructure and web applications, on a plan a small team would realistically buy.
  3. Does it help decide what to fix first? Some signal beyond a raw CVSS score, and enough detail to act on a finding without reproducing it from scratch.
  4. What happens after the fix? Rescans that confirm it, a status history, and a route into Jira, Slack or similar.

Paid plans add emerging threat scans, which check your estate when a new flaw goes public instead of waiting for the next scheduled run. They also add authenticated web app and API testing, daily cloud checks across AWS, Azure and Google Cloud, and integrations such as Jira and Slack.

Best for: Small teams that want external, web and cloud coverage with little setup and a clear fix order.

Trade-off: The free plan leaves out web apps and monitors only ports 80 and 443. Internal and agent-based scanning starts at the Pro plan, which goes through sales, and automated discovery of unknown assets sits in Enterprise.

2. Aikido Security

Aikido starts from the repository. Dependency scanning, static analysis and secrets detection run alongside DAST, container scanning, infrastructure-as-code and cloud misconfiguration checks in one account. Paid plans add web application scanning and, for perimeter findings, SLA timers that start at first detection. On the free plan, one host gets a weekly scan alongside one repository and one user, and a 14-day trial of a paid plan needs no card.

Best for: Teams where a DevOps lead or CTO owns security among other things and wants the perimeter and code under one subscription.

Trade-off: There is no internal network scanning, because hosts need a public address to be scanned. Cloud integration covers AWS only, and Slack, Microsoft Teams and Jira routing isn’t on the entry-level paid plan.

4. HostedScan

HostedScan runs established engines so you don’t have to: OpenVAS, OWASP ZAP, Nuclei, Nmap and SSLyze on every plan, with Nessus on the top tier. The Exploit plan adds Sniper, an automatic CVE exploiter, which comes in handy when an engineer asks for proof that a finding is real.

Best for: A team with some offensive security experience that wants to validate findings itself.

For a small team, the payload is the useful part, because the finding shows what triggered it. The Starter tier has no platform fee and allows up to five users.

Best for: SaaS companies whose exposure is mainly web apps, APIs and a sprawl of subdomains.

Trade-off: Surface Monitoring and Application Scanning are billed per domain and per target, in addition to any platform fee. Internal scanning starts at the Professional tier, and tiers above Starter go through a demo or sales.
